I sit through a lot of presentations, and I usually know inside the first three minutes whether I am going to learn anything. It is not about the English. It is about the order. If the first slide is a map of the organisation, I already know the number is coming on slide fourteen, and by then I have read my email twice. So here is what those three minutes should contain. Say who you are, in one line. Give me the outline, so that I know what is coming and I can stop guessing. Then give me the headline, the one number or the one message, before any of the detail that explains it. And tell me when you want questions, because if you do not tell me, I will interrupt you and you will lose your place. One last thing, since nobody ever says it out loud. I am not going to remember your accent. I have never once walked out of a meeting thinking about somebody's accent. I remember whether the person knew which thing mattered.

My first presentation in English was eleven slides long, and I rehearsed every single word of it. I wrote the whole script, I read it about forty times, and I still remember standing there with my mouth completely dry. Here is what I learned that day. Rehearsing the words was the wrong preparation. The sentences came out differently anyway, and that turned out to be fine. What saved me was the outline. I had said, in the first minute, that I would walk them through three things, and every time I lost myself I looked at that list and found my place again. The second thing that saved me was a backup slide. Somebody asked for a number I had left out, and instead of apologising for four sentences, I said, I have that here, and I showed it. That was the moment the room started treating me as somebody who knew the business. So do not rehearse the sentences. Rehearse the order, and prepare for the one question you are afraid of.

Good morning, everyone, and thank you for the floor. I am Renato, Commercial Manager for the South and Southeast of Brazil. I will walk you through three things today: the quarter, the interior of Sao Paulo, and what I need from you. The headline is that we have grown in both regions, but the interior is still the gap. I would like to keep the Q and A for the last five minutes.
